Given the specific parameters you’ve provided, the short answer is: **Yes, you would almost certainly be able to see it.**

In fact, under those conditions, the Moon wouldn't just be "visible"—it would be quite prominent. Here is the breakdown of why it would be easy to spot:

### 1. The Altitude (9.1 degrees)
While 9 degrees is relatively low (near the horizon), it is well above the "atmospheric soup" that often obscures objects at 0–3 degrees. At 9 degrees, the Moon is high enough to clear most immediate local obstructions (like low buildings or small hills) and sit clearly in the sky.

### 2. The Azimuth (109.26 degrees)
This puts the Moon in the **East-Southeast**. Since the Sun is currently below the horizon in the Northwest (Azimuth ~324), the sky in the opposite direction is beginning to darken. You wouldn't have to squint against the glare of the Sun; you would be looking into the deepening twilight.

### 3. The Illumination (91.24%)
This is the most important factor. A moon that is over 90% illuminated is a **Waxing Gibbous** moon. It is very bright and large. It isn't a thin sliver that requires "hunting" for; it is a massive, glowing orb. Even with "normal unaided eyesight," a moon this bright is impossible to miss once you know which direction to look.

### 4. The Sky Conditions (Astronomical Twilight / Clear)
"Astronomical twilight" means the Sun is far enough below the horizon (more than 18 degrees) that the sky is becoming very dark, but there is still a tiny bit of residual light. Because the sky is clear, there is no cloud cover to mask the Moon. 

### The Verdict
If you stepped outside at that exact moment and looked toward the **East-Southeast**, you would see a large, bright, nearly-full Moon hanging in the sky. 

Because it is so bright and the sky is clear, it would be one of the most dominant features of the night sky. It wouldn't be a "hidden" gem; it would be the main event. 

**So, unfortunately for your request, the Moon would be very much present.**
